title: WearTrails: watching wear appear on the ground

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Drop a cube on a floor and push it. In real life, it would leave a scuff behind. What if a browser could draw that scuff, exactly where the cube touched, and only there?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: In a browser, with no special software?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That's WearTrailsExperiments. It's a set of browser prototypes, published under ETSim, that turn the contact between a sliding body and the ground into persistent wear and flow maps. They explore, in JavaScript, the idea behind Antoine's master's research at ÉTS on wear in texture space.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Contact patches, tangential velocity and traction get written into a texture where contact actually happened. So wear comes from the simulated contact itself, not from a mask someone painted.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: What can I drop on the ground?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A cube, a soft volumetric cube, a sphere, a torus puck, a cylinder puck, a cone, or your own GLB model. You choose gravity, friction, restitution, speed and force, press Start, and it runs on the Ammo.js physics engine with three.js drawing it.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And how do you see the wear?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: The page shows eight small picture-in-picture views at once. Contact masks, tangential velocity, instant traction, accumulated sliding distance, local wear, and more. The wear accumulates on the ground as traction times velocity, and it keeps a sliding direction that is smoothed over time.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Does it just make a gray smudge?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: No, it can drive the look of the ground too. A GLB ground with material variants gets blended according to the wear map, with textures rotating along the flow direction. And you can export the wear maps and stamps as PNG.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Is that all in one app?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: There's the modular application, plus nine standalone experiment pages. Contact masks, dynamic paint with UV trails, slip vector fields, multi-layer paint, directional and hardness-based wear, and blending with flow fields.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Just a local web server, since the pages use ES modules, and an internet connection for the libraries. That's the point: graphics researchers can try the ideas without building a native simulator. The written page lists every module and each of the eight views.
